transcript.text: I am the operations lead at a tour company. Each month I tell our local partners how many guides to reserve in each destination for the month after next. If I reserve too few, we hire freelancers at the last minute for about three times the price; if I reserve too many, we pay a small fee for each guide we do not use. My director asked me for a machine learning model that forecasts how many bookings we will receive per destination each month. The table I shared is our booking export up to late February 2026: one row per booking with the booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. I will use the result myself every month to fix the reservation. [shares bookings.csv]

Two things to check before I propose anything: your booking curve and the export's limits.

Here's what I read from your export before saying anything about the model — then three ways to start.

**The problem, as I understand it.** You don't actually need "how many bookings we will receive next month." You need, for the travel month you're reserving for, how many people will *show up* — and you have to commit two months before you know it. So you're committing to roughly a third of volume you can't yet see. That's the real forecasting job.

**Four things that need care before any model runs.**

1. *The export is cut off mid-curve.* Bookings stop at 24 Feb 2026, but travel dates run to Aug 2026, so "bookings per travel month" collapses at the end (109 in Mar 2026, then 78, 67, 33, 23, 8). A model trained on raw monthly counts would learn a fake decline. Only travel months fully closed (Mar 2025–Jan 2026) can be training targets.
2. *Cancelled bookings shouldn't count, but cancellation status is also still moving for future months* — overall cancellation runs at 0.23, so sizing on gross bookings would over-reserve by about a quarter.
3. *A point forecast is the wrong deliverable for your costs.* Freelancers cost ~3x, idle guides cost a small fee. The cheap answer isn't "the most likely number," it's a number with an uncertainty band, and you reserve at a percentile set by that ratio. A model that only gives a mean will make you overpay either way.
4. So no shuffling rows into train/test — validation has to go forward in time, and a simple seasonal rule is the benchmark the ML must beat. Also: 12 rows are marked destination TEST, which I'll drop, and the export has no travellers-per-booking, so the model gives bookings and you convert to guides with your own ratio. One caution: nationality and channel are useful demand signals for sizing, but nothing here should end up as guidance to partners about which travellers to accept.

**The ways to go.** *Baseline curve first* — cheap, usable this month, and it becomes the yardstick. *Straight to the ML model* — what your director asked for; better if late bookings vary month to month, but needs the baseline to prove it. *A recurring dashboard* — you refresh monthly, no model yet.

I recommend the baseline first, then the model — the model's value is exactly the gain over the baseline, and that's the number your director will want.

**The plan**
1. Clean: drop TEST rows, define a kept booking, and build one row per destination × travel month with, for each, the count already on the books 2 months out and the eventual kept total.
2. Baseline: per destination, the average share of the eventual total that arrives inside the 2-month window, plus month-of-year pattern. Check: apply it to months it never saw and measure error.
3. Model: forecast kept bookings per destination for the travel month two ahead, using the on-the-books count, calendar, and channel/nationality mix, with a time-ordered holdout. Check: it must beat the baseline on the same holdout.
4. Cost sizing: translate the forecast's error band into a recommended reservation at your 3x-vs-small-fee ratio, and show the cost saved versus always reserving the point forecast. Check: expected cost, stated in your own price units.
5. Handover: a monthly view you refresh yourself before calling the partners. Check: it reproduces two past decisions you remember making.
6. Stop when the model beats the baseline on the forward holdout and gives you a reservation number you'd defend to your director.
7. If a step fails: if history is too thin to beat the baseline, I'll tell you and we keep the baseline plus a safety-stock rule, which still answers your decision.

The three choices are above. My advice is the first one now and the second right after: the baseline gives you a defensible reserve number for the next call with your partners, and it's the yardstick that proves whether the ML model earns its keep — that comparison is the sentence your director will actually care about.

Pick one and I'll run its first step straight away.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

| Destination | On books two months out | Kept in the end | Cancellations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paris | 134 | 158 | 19.4% |
| Bangkok | 134 | 152 | 24.4% |
| Istanbul | 117 | 141 | 20.8% |
| Dubai | 126 | 140 | 25.5% |
| London | 129 | 139 | 24.0% |

Next quarter my team can run at most three email campaigns: one to move people to a higher plan, one to keep people who look likely to leave, and one welcome series for new customers. The same person should not receive two of them. My campaign managers will use the segments to decide who gets which campaign. [shares customers.csv]

Understood: the board wants names on a slide, but the real job is a targeting rule — five or six segments that your campaign managers can sort into three mutually exclusive emails (upgrade, retention, welcome) next quarter. So I'll judge the segmentation by whether each segment has one obvious campaign and one measurable outcome, not by how tidy the clusters look.

What your table already says: 1,200 customers, 17.4% churn the next month overall. The recorded segment column is only business (239, churn 14.6%) versus consumer (961, churn 18.1%) — it barely separates anything, so a new segmentation earns its place. Plan does most of the work today: basic 603 (churn 22.4%), plus 369 (11.1%), premium 228 (14.5%). Only 53 customers have tenure of 3 months or less, and monthly_spend is missing on 48 rows.

Three things need care before any work:

1. **churned_next_month cannot be an input.** It is only known a month after the fact, so any segment defined by it cannot be applied to today's list. I'll build segments from what you know before sending (tenure, plan, spend, tickets, signup date) and use the churn column afterwards to check whether the segments really separate risk.
2. **The welcome segment will not appear on its own.** 53 of 1,200 people are new; a clustering that finds 5–6 balanced groups will swallow them into someone else. The new-customer group needs a tenure rule, decided up front — and I need to know where "new" stops (3 months? 6?).
3. **City is a poor segment input.** Churn ranges from 11.8% in Ras Al Khaimah to 21.2% in Sharjah, but a segment that is really geography invites offers differing by location. I'd keep city for reading the results, not for forming the groups. The 48 customers with no spend figure I'd keep, flagged as spend unknown, rather than drop — dropping them means they get no campaign at all.

Three ways to solve it, and my pick:

- **Behavioural clustering on the four usable features**, then overlay churn to name and validate the groups: fastest to a slide, genuinely data-driven, but the retention group is only as good as spend/tickets/tenure predict leaving. This is my pick for a first pass.
- **A churn-risk score first, then risk-by-value segments:** sharper for the retention campaign and it can be rescored monthly, but it is a model project — more work, and it needs your sign-off before building.
- **Rules in SQL on plan and tenure:** deliverable this week and fully explainable, but it is your old segmentation with extra steps, and won't look like AI to the board.

The plan:

2. Cluster on tenure, monthly spend, plan and support tickets, plus a new-customer flag, targeting 6 groups, each customer in exactly one. Checked by group sizes and by how far apart the groups are on spend and churn.
3. Validate each group against churned_next_month and mean spend, then name them (upgrade-ready, at-risk, welcome, and so on). Checked by the retention group showing churn well above 17.4% without having been built from it.
4. Map groups to your three campaigns with a priority order — welcome, then retention, then upgrade — so no one appears twice, and a residual group gets no email. Checked by the campaign counts adding to 1,200.
5. Deliver the segment table and a one-slide view for the board.

transcript.text: I am a data scientist at a company that sells accounting software to small firms. Two years ago we built a model that scores every new lead on how likely it is to become a customer, and the sales team calls the highest scores first. Since the autumn the sales team says the top leads are much worse than they used to be, and my manager wants me to retrain with a larger model and more features. Some context on the data: since the summer, part of our leads comes from a partner marketplace; we moved to a new CRM in August, and two form fields the model uses are no longer collected; and finance now counts a lead as converted when a free trial starts, where before it was the first payment. I have the old training set and every lead since, not yet exported. What would you do?

**What I think is actually wrong**

You've been handed a fix — a bigger model, more features — for a symptom that four separate data changes can produce on their own. The biggest one is your target. Since autumn, "converted" means a started free trial; before, it meant a first payment. Those are different populations, with trial starts being more numerous and looser. A model trained to rank predicted *payments* is now being judged against predicted *trials*, and it will look bad in the top of the list even if it has not changed at all. Two of the fields it scores on also stopped being collected, and whatever the pipeline fills in for them (nulls, defaults, imputed values) silently re-ranks every lead — that's the kind of break that shows up as "the good leads got worse" with no error anywhere. Add a marketplace source whose leads look nothing like the old training population, and a CRM migration that may not join cleanly across August, and you have several candidate causes pointing at measurement, not capacity.

So the risk in doing what was asked is real: a larger model fits a half-way-changed label better, scores smoothly, and tells you nothing about what actually shifted. You'd lose the diagnosis and the ability to ever get it back.

**What needs care before any work**

- Don't pool old and new conversions into one target column, even though it's tempting to "just add more history."
- Judge the top of the list separately for marketplace versus your own leads, and before versus after August. A pooled average will hide whichever group is really broken.
- Check whether the ranking got worse mostly where the two dropped fields are missing — that's the cheapest smoking gun you have.
- Expect selection bias: sales calls the high scores, so you mostly observe outcomes for leads you already called. Any "conversion rate by score" you compare across periods is partly a story about sales behaviour.
- Agree which definition of converted you are predicting — finance's new one, or the one sales is complaining about — before you pick features or a loss.

**Ways to solve it**

*Diagnose first (my choice).* Split the drop by period, source and missing-field status on both label definitions. It's a day of work on lead-level data and it tells you whether you need a new model or a fixed pipeline — and it gives your manager a defensible answer either way. *Retrain on the new label.* Fast and it satisfies the ask, but if the cause is a broken feature or a shifted source, the new model inherits the same blindness with more parameters. *Build a monitoring/segmentation layer instead.* Best long-run value, weakest on the immediate complaint. A bigger model is the one thing on this list that can't tell you which problem you have.

The plan

1. You export lead-level rows: lead id, date created, source (marketplace or not), the model's score at the time if stored, both outcome dates (trial start, first payment) if both exist, plus the model's input features including the two dropped fields. This gives the raw material for every later step.
2. I check what that table can actually answer — whether both labels survive on the same leads, whether scores are point-in-time, and where the August CRM break cuts the history. This decides which diagnoses are possible at all.
3. We rebuild the outcome two ways (payment, trial) and compare how the top of the list looks on each, by month. This separates "the model changed" from "the bar changed."
4. We decompose the decline by source and by missing-field status, month by month. This names the segment or field responsible, rather than guessing.
5. We test score quality per segment on a post-change time split — ranking only, no retraining. This shows whether the current model is still useful where it had enough input.
6. Only then we retrain, on the agreed label, with a feature set that exists at scoring time, evaluated on that post-change split and reported by segment. Success means the top slice converts better than today's model on the same leads and period, not a higher overall score.

Stop when we can point to which of the four changes explains most of the drop, and your manager has that in writing with the retrain recommendation attached. If a step fails — for instance payment dates no longer exist for recent leads — we say so and switch the target to the earliest outcome you can still observe consistently across the break, rather than blending definitions.

Whichever route you take, start that export now. Meanwhile, here's how I'd begin — pick the one that fits what your manager needs this week:

One thing decides which of those routes is even possible, so tell me this first: for your recent leads, can you still recover *both* outcome dates — the started-trial date finance uses now, and the first-payment date the old model was trained on? Or did the payment date disappear from the CRM history when finance changed the definition?
Everything I know is in what I wrote. Choose what you judge best and go ahead.

Diagnosis-first is what I chose — a larger model can't tell you which of your four changes caused the drop, so we find that out before we retrain. I'm on **step 1: the export**, and nothing else can run until it lands. **Send me one row per lead, over the whole period, with:**

- `lead_id`, plus the old-CRM id and new-CRM id if they differ after the August move — the join across the migration is the first thing I need to verify, not assume. - `created_at`, and `source` / channel with an explicit marketplace flag. - **The score the model actually gave at scoring time**, with `scored_at` and the model or feature version. No imputation in the export; the imputer is a suspect, not a cleaning step. - `trial_started_at` and `first_payment_at` as raw event dates, both nullable. - Sales contact fields if the CRM keeps them — called, call date, disposition. I'm assuming finance's new trial definition has already been applied retroactively to that flag, which would quietly rewrite history; I'd rather rebuild both targets from the dates and see whether they disagree. CSV or Parquet both work. Once it's shared, step 2 is my coverage check: do both labels survive on the same leads, is the score point-in-time, and exactly where does August cut the history — then the label comparison by month.

transcript.text: I am the credit risk manager at a consumer lender that finances phone and appliance purchases in shops. Today a rulebook written by our underwriters approves about 40 percent of applications. Management wants to grow, so they asked me for a machine learning model that predicts default for every applicant, to replace the rulebook and approve more people safely. We have about 60,000 past loans with the application form, the bureau score and whether the loan defaulted within 12 months, and I can export them next week. For the applications we rejected we kept the form and the bureau score, nothing more. The model would decide each new application automatically at the shop counter. How should I go about it?

[DCLab drew a dashboard above this message]

Understood, and the shape of it is clear: management wants growth, you were handed "build a model," and the model is meant to be the decision at the counter. I'd like to put one thing in front of that before anything is built, because it changes the whole sequence. A blueprint card is now shown beside this message — its cost numbers are placeholders, not your numbers.

**What needs care before any work starts**

Your 60,000 loans are all loans you *said yes to*. A model trained on that book and pointed at every applicant is guessing about precisely the people management wants to approve, and no test on this export can prove it right there. In backtest it will flatter you; in production it will be the one place you have no evidence.

Three smaller things follow from that:

- "Approve more safely" is not an accuracy question. AUC or KS won't tell you what the marginal fifth of new approvals costs.
- A 12-month default flag only exists on accounts matured 12 months, so recent originations must be set aside, and validation must split by application date, never randomly.
- Automating at the counter without a human usually brings adverse-action reasons, independent validation, drift and fair-lending monitoring, and a fallback path. Application-form fields like address, employer or device type can act as proxies for protected characteristics, so the rulebook disappearing is a governance event, not just a technical one.

**Ways it could be solved**

A business brief first: what the current 40% costs, and how far you can *provably* push it with the data you have — cheap, gives management a defensible answer this month, builds nothing. The model now on the funded book: a proper scorecard with a time-ordered holdout and a swap analysis against the rulebook — real output, but it can only rank people inside the population you already lend to until rejects get outcomes. Preparation first: fix the export and design a way to learn about rejects (documented overrides, or approving a small random slice of rulebook rejects) — slowest to a headline, but it's the only route that eventually makes the growth claim honest.

I'd take the brief first, then build the model on top of it, so the model answers a priced question rather than a mandate.

**The plan**

1. Pull four real numbers from your book: default rate on matured loans, average margin and loss given default per funded loan, monthly application volume. Checked against the export row counts.
2. Specify next week's export: application date, form fields, bureau score and its version, the rulebook decision, any override, default flag and account age. Rejections stay in a separate table, not dropped.
3. Build the scorecard on matured funded loans, holdout = the latest months by application date. Checked by realised default rate per risk decile on the holdout, monotone and consistent with trend.
4. Close the reject gap: reject inference, plus a small randomised or exception approval of rulebook rejects, so their predicted risk can be compared with what they actually do.
5. Pick the approval line in money: loss-versus-approval-rate curve and a swap set showing who is newly approved and newly declined versus the rulebook. Checked by management signing a stated loss budget.
6. Only then automate: reason codes, human review path, system-outage fallback, independent validation, drift and fair-lending monitoring during a shadow period.

Stop when an approval line is chosen against a signed loss budget, with the automation sign-off documented. If a step fails — typically step 4, if randomised approvals aren't permitted — the model stays decision support inside your current lending population and the "approve more" claim is dropped from the project rather than assumed.

Two of those are on screen for you to pick. The scorecard route didn't appear because there's no table in the case yet — column names can't be promised against data I haven't seen; it becomes available once you've shared the export, and I'd build it as step 3 of the plan after one of these.

If it helps you choose: the brief is what you take into the next management meeting, the preparation is what makes next week's export worth something. They're both worth doing, and I'd start with the brief unless your team is already pressing you for the export specification.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

One more check on the blank amounts, then I'll lay out the picture.

A gap of about nine percent is exactly what a definitional difference of this size produces, not an arithmetic error. **What needs care before Monday.**

Build the dashboard now with every tile labelled by definition and gross/paid/net shown side by side, so neither team is "wrong" — fastest, but it only holds if finance signs the headline measure. Monday pack: definition page plus the three-totals bridge as the cover. Stop when finance and sales have both accepted the headline measure in writing. If a step fails, publish the dashboard with all three totals labelled rather than forcing one number.

Two of those are now in front of you: the labelled dashboard, or the governed base table first. My recommendation is the dashboard, because the reconciliation evidence is already in this chat and can sit on the tiles as a definition note — but if you think finance will contest the headline measure in the room, take the clean base table first so the numbers under it are settled. transcript.text: I am the commercial director of a building-materials distributor. Last year we bought a competitor, so we now have two customer lists: about 4,000 accounts in our system and 2,500 in theirs. I want a customer lifetime value model on the combined list so we know which accounts deserve a key-account manager; we can afford one for about 150 accounts. Each system has its own account numbers. Company names were typed by hand, the same contractor often has a separate account for each building site or branch, and many firms bought from both of us. Both systems hold three years of invoices with the account number, date and amount. Nothing is exported yet. My sales reps say the big customers are obvious and the list should find the ones they miss.

**What you're really asking for**

A shortlist of the ~150 customer *firms* most worth a key-account manager, built from two systems that count customers differently, so you can also see the ones your field team doesn't currently rate. Two things you told me decide the whole design: the same contractor holds several accounts (one per site or branch), and many firms bought from both of you. So the model isn't the hard part; the merge is.

**What needs care before any work**

- **Grain.** Value must be computed at firm level, with accounts and sites kept underneath so you can see how each firm's spend is spread and who owns which relationship.
- **Matching is not neutral.** Hand-typed names won't match reliably on their own. A bad merge either gives one firm two managers or, worse, strips a genuinely large customer of one because its revenue got split across unmatched records. Every automatic match needs a confidence level and a review pile — and your reps, who know the firms, should clear that pile, not a script.
- **Turnover is not profit.** Invoices give amount only. Margins in building materials vary hugely, so a revenue ranking favours bulk commodity buyers over smaller, profitable accounts.
Concentration needs flagging, not hiding.
- **Acquisition effect.** Three years of history straddles the deal; price, coverage and reps changed midway, so recent trend must be weighed separately from lifetime totals.

**Ways it could be done**

1. *Rank accounts on three-year revenue* — days of work, wrong grain, and it only rediscovers the obvious big names.
2. *Merge to firms, then rank on observed value plus a forward-looking CLV* — the sound version of what you asked for; a few weeks including the merge review.
3. *Merge to firms, then score for under-served potential* (value + growth + no active coverage + concentration risk) — this is the one that actually finds who your reps miss, built on the same foundation as 2.

I recommend 2 leading straight into 3: the merge is unavoidable either way, and a value ranking without the coverage view won't earn your reps' trust.

**The plan**

1. **Export spec + identifier check.** Define exactly what to pull from both systems (invoices *and* customer master files). Checked by row counts and totals matching each system's own revenue reports.
2. **Entity resolution.** Build the firm table from tax/VAT number where present, then name/address matching; three confidence tiers, reps clear the middle.
3. **Value baseline.** Firm-level revenue, order count, months active, recency, share by site, growth before/after the acquisition. Checked by reconciling to both systems.
4. That hit-rate is the honest test.
5. **Shortlist of 150** with reason codes and risk flags (project-concentrated, declining, uncertain merge), plus a count of names the reps hadn't flagged.
6. **Quarterly refresh** so the list stays alive rather than being a one-off.

Stop when: 150 named firms carry value, growth and risk flags, revenue reconciles to both systems, and the reps have signed off the uncertain merges. If a step fails: if no firm-level identifier exists in both systems, we publish fuzzy matches with a confidence band and a review queue instead of one clean list.

**One thing blocks step 1:** in the two *customer master* files (not the invoices), is there anything firm-level you can export for every account — VAT/tax registration number, billing address, parent-company code — and does each account carry an assigned rep?

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)
Everything I know is in what I wrote. Choose what you judge best and go ahead.

**Step 1 — the export spec.** Nothing can be modelled until the two systems speak the same language, so this is the file list to hand to IT. Four files, plus one more if it exists. *File 1 and 2 — invoices, one per system (legacy, acquired):*
account number · invoice number · invoice date · line net amount (excl. VAT, your base currency, credit notes as negative rows or a document-type column) · product group or category code, if the line carries one · ship-to address or site name · the taking rep / branch code, if stamped on the invoice. Full three years, all document states, **line level if the system can give it, otherwise invoice-level totals** — say which you sent. *File 3 and 4 — customer master, one per system:*
account number · legal name · trading name · VAT/tax registration number · billing address (street, city, postcode, country) · any parent-company or account-group code · assigned rep or branch · customer type (trade counter vs contract vs retail) · account open date · status and closed date · credit limit. *File 5, if it exists in any form:* which accounts already carry a key-account manager or named rep. If no such list survives the acquisition, tell me and I'll infer coverage from rep codes on invoices instead — the "who your reps miss" view depends on it, the value ranking does not. **Format:** CSV, UTF-8, one file per system per table, dates as YYYY-MM-DD, amounts as plain decimals with no thousands separators or currency symbols, no pivot tables or subtotals baked in. Strip anything you don't need — but keep ship-to address and VAT number; they are the whole merge. **Also send, so I can prove the data arrived intact:** per system, the number of invoice rows and total revenue for each of the three years, as your own reports state it. I reconcile against those before a single firm is matched. **What happens when the files land here.** I build the pipeline: standardise names and addresses, then match accounts to firms on VAT number where present, otherwise name-plus-address, and split the result into high-confidence firms, low-confidence firms and a review pile for your reps. Your first output is not a list of 150 — it's the shape check: how many accounts collapse into how many firms, how many firms trade with both businesses, what share of revenue sits in each confidence tier, and whether the totals tie to your reports. transcript.text: I am the revenue manager of a travel agency that sells in the UAE and, since last year, to customers in Europe through our website. Cancellations cost us a lot, so I plan to ask for a non-refundable deposit from the bookings most likely to be cancelled and keep the normal terms for everyone else. Please build the model that decides who must pay the deposit. The table I shared has one row per booking: booking date, travel date, destination, the customer's nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether free cancellation was offered, and whether the booking was cancelled. From what I have seen in our reports, nationality tells the most about who cancels, so I expect it to be the main input. The website would apply the rule automatically at checkout. [shares bookings.csv]

Here is what I understood, one thing I would change before building, and how I'd run it. **Your decision, as I read it:** you want to stop absorbing the cost of cancellations by charging a non-refundable deposit only to the bookings most likely to cancel, applied automatically at checkout, with everyone else on normal terms. That is a sensible, narrow rule — and the table can support it: 1,500 bookings, 343 cancellations, 22.9%. **What needs care before any model is built.** I won't build this one with customer nationality as the main input, and I'd urge you not to ship it as the rule either. A deposit is a term of trade: demanding more from someone because of their nationality is direct discrimination on a protected characteristic, in your EU market and in the UAE, and an automatic checkout decision that changes what a person must pay is exactly the kind of decision a regulator or an aggrieved customer will ask you to explain. "Our reports show nationality predicts it" is also the standard shape of a disparate-impact finding, not a defence. The data makes this easier than you might expect, because nationality is your *weakest* signal, not your strongest. Destination is middling (Dubai 26.2%, Paris 18.9%); channel is flat (22.6%, 22.6%, 23.8%); and whether free cancellation was offered barely matters (23.3% vs 22.6%). You can get a better rule from booking features you are entitled to use — how far ahead, where, when, at what price. Three more things I found that must be fixed first: `price` has arrived as text rather than numbers, there are 12 rows with destination `TEST`, and a booking only earns its "cancelled" label once its travel date has passed, so the most recent months (bookings run to 2026-02-24) are partly unlabelled and would drag a model's accuracy down falsely. **The plan**

1. Prepare the table: convert price to a number, set aside the `TEST` rows, and cut a training window where travel dates have passed so outcomes are final. Check: row counts before and after, with your yes on anything that removes many rows. 2. Measure the honest drivers and the money at stake: cancellation rates by lead time, destination, price band, channel, season and repeat-customer status, and how much of the 343 cancellations sit in the top slice of risk. Check: each segment is large enough to read, and one feature's effect is not just a shadow of another. 3. Set the base rate you would need to beat, then build the risk score on booking features only, on a time-ordered holdout (the future, never shuffled). Check: it beats the base rate on bookings it has never seen. 4. Test the finished rule two ways — does it just re-derive nationality, and how much revenue does the deposit actually protect at each threshold. Check: a clear statement of who pays, how often, and what it costs you in lost bookings. 5. Write the checkout wording and the human-review route for anyone refused normal terms. Stop when you have a threshold you can defend in public, plus the measured cancellation risk of the group it charges. If a step fails — the model can't beat the base rate, or the score turns out to be a nationality proxy in disguise — we come back to you with that finding, and the fairer two-fare design becomes the main route rather than the alternative. Choose where to begin below. My recommendation is the first one: it is quick, it settles the data problems, and it tells you whether a model is even worth the effort before you promise a checkout rule to your web team.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

choices.title: Find what really predicts a cancellation, and what it is worth
choices.what: A report on your cleaned booking table: cancellation risk by lead time, destination, price band, channel, season and repeat-customer status, plus how much of the loss sits in the top slice of risk. It also measures, as a check, how differently any rule would land by nationality without ever using nationality as an input. You get: A defensible list of booking features you can lawfully charge on, the size of the prize, and the base rate a model would have to beat. Trade-off: No new rule goes live from this step alone; it is the evidence that makes the rule safe to build. Effort: Low — one session on the table you already shared.

choices.title: Cancellation-risk model for the checkout deposit, on legitimate booking features only
choices.what: A trained score for 'this booking will be cancelled', built from lead time, destination, price, travel season, channel and booking history. Customer nationality is left out of the inputs entirely; the finished score is then tested for whether it simply re-creates nationality. You get: The automatic checkout rule you asked for, in a form that stands up to a complaint or a regulator's question. Trade-off: Slightly less accuracy in theory than using every column; the data suggests the loss is small, because nationality is your weakest signal here. Effort: Medium — preparation, a time-based holdout, then threshold setting.

choices.title: Reprice the choice instead of screening the person
choices.what: A business brief on the deposit policy itself: everyone is offered the same two fares — a lower non-refundable one and a flexible one at a surcharge, set per route and lead-time band from your own cancellation rates. Risk is priced into the product, not into the customer. You get: Most of the cancellation protection with no personal characteristic in the decision, and a design that is easy to explain at checkout. Trade-off: It depends on customers choosing, and on you being allowed to run two fares in the UAE and EU markets. Effort: Medium — analysis of rates plus a written policy and price grid.

transcript.text: I am an analyst at an online retailer in the UAE. Please build a model that predicts, at the moment an order is placed, whether it will end in a refund. The table I shared is our order export, one row per order: order_id, order_date, region, channel, product_category, amount, status and customer_id. The status column shows how each order ended. Refunds are only possible within 14 days, and the export was taken six weeks after the last order in it, so every status is final. The customer care team will score each new order as it comes in and phone the buyers of the riskiest ones to confirm the product and delivery details before we ship. Go ahead. [shares sales.csv]

Understood, and the data supports what you asked for. Here is my read, in your terms:

**The problem.** You want, at the moment of checkout, a refund risk score for every order, so customer care can phone the riskiest buyers before shipping and cut refunds at the source. The label is clean: 2,020 orders, 1,733 paid, 188 refunded, 99 cancelled — a base refund rate of 9.3% — and since refunds close within 14 days while the export came six weeks after the last order (2025-01-01 to 2026-03-31), every row has its final answer. Nothing in the table was written after the outcome, and amount is not a refund in disguise (mean 232.65 on refunded orders against 241.58 on paid ones; the 50 rows with a missing amount refund at 8.0%, close to the overall 9.3%). **What needs care before the work is judged.**
- `status` has three endings, not two. A cancelled order never ships, so no confirmation call can happen for it. Correct me if a cancelled order can still turn into a refund. - Split by time, never at random. With 1,002 customers across 2,000 order ids, a shuffled split lets a customer's later refund sit in the training set and inflate the score. Test on the most recent months only, and build any customer-history feature from strictly earlier orders. - Where the cut sits is a capacity question, not a statistical one. Refund rates run from 12.2% in Ajman to 4.1% in Ras Al Khaimah, so a top-N list concentrates calls in a few emirates and starves others; I will check that balance rather than hide it. - This table cannot tell you whether the calls worked — no record of contact or of a prevented refund. Proving the value needs a small held-back group that gets no call. **Ways to solve it.** Simple rules on category, region and amount: cheap and explainable, but a ceiling on accuracy. A three-class model including cancellation: more work, same call list. A binary gradient-boosted model on placed-order features plus that customer's prior behaviour, judged on precision at the number of calls you can actually make: what I am choosing, because it matches how you will use it, and a rules baseline will be kept beside it so you can see whether the model earns its place. The plan:
1. Check: row counts and refund rate before and after. 2. Set the target: refunded = 1 among non-cancelled orders. Check: base rate is stable across months. 3. Build features available at placement: region, channel, product_category, amount, order timing, plus each customer's prior order count, prior refunds, days since last order — computed only from earlier orders. Check: a leakage pass on every derived column. 4. Split by time: train on the earlier months, test on the latest. Check: no customer straddles the boundary in a way that leaks. 5. Train the model and compare it with the rules baseline on the held-out period only. Check: it must beat the baseline, or we ship the baseline. 6. Check: you pick the cut. 7. Package for scoring new orders, with a monthly drift watch on the refund rate. Stop when: a tested model beats the baseline on the most recent months and its top-N call list fits your team's daily capacity. If a step fails: if the lift is small we keep the rules list and tell you plainly, and any cleaning that removes an unexpected number of rows comes back to you before it is applied. DCLab is checking the remaining build requirements now; I will not quote a result until it has run. One thing that would sharpen the final report: roughly how many confirmation calls can the care team make per day?
